rationale: The frame is a census of the single high-security hospital serving Scotland and Northern Ireland: 'a whole population cohort of 241 patients ... detained within the high secure State Hospital, Carstairs, Scotland, at some point between 25th August 1992 and 13th August 1993'. It is complete for people requiring high-security forensic care, which is the authors' own target population ('What happened to patients who required high secure care in 1992/93'). It does not address people with psychosis generally: the Introduction describes detention of individuals 'with a history of serious violence and who pose a grave risk to the public', only 70 per cent (169 of 241) had a primary diagnosis of schizophrenia at baseline, and the employment result is reported for the consenting cohort as a whole, not for the schizophrenia subgroup. The frame is recruitment in high-security care, not detention at the outcome assessment: among those with location data, 56.0 per cent 'experienced at least some time in the community/possibly prison' and 12.0 per cent never left high security.

rationale: 241 entered and the employment result rests on 56 living consented participants (author reply; the paper prints no denominator for this outcome, and Table 1 gives 66 consenting). No sample size calculation or precision target is stated, and the cohort size was fixed by the hospital population. No interval is given for the employment proportion; 0 of 56 carries an exact binomial 95 per cent interval of 0 to roughly 6.4 per cent. The judgement is provisional: the review has no common precision criterion for this item, so adequacy is judged only on what the paper says, which is nothing.

rationale: Table 1 describes the baseline cohort of 241 (sex, mean age and range by sex, primary diagnosis, comorbid ASPD, mean lifetime inpatient stay) and the Scottish forensic pathway and its security levels are described in detail. The people who carry the employment result are not described: no age, sex or diagnosis is given for the consenting group, and their place of residence at assessment (high, medium, low or open security, or community), which governs access to the labour market, is not tabulated. Partial indications are that keyworkers of '24 individuals resident in the community at the time of the invitation to study' supplied relationship data; that qualitative interviews were analysed for 10 participants resident in high or medium security, 10 in low or open wards and 10 in the community at the 20 year follow-up, so each setting contributed at least 10 of the 48 interviewed; that half of the 10 community interviewees were 'living in supported accommodation or receiving a comprehensive support package within their own homes' and 80 per cent of them had a baseline primary diagnosis of schizophrenia; and that the group contributing data 'demonstrated higher median scores' for baseline age and length of inpatient stay. Fuller description is deferred to earlier publications.

rationale: Table 1 records 89 of 241 deceased by 31 December 2017, leaving about 152 survivors (153 on Table 1's non-deceased categories, which include one person who died after participating). Of these, gatekeepers approved 87 for invitation; 37 were judged to lack capacity or to be too unwell, 21 lived outside Scotland with no gatekeeper information, 4 had no appropriate gatekeeper and 4 were lost. Table 1 gives 66 consenting; the author reply gives 56 living consented participants for the employment outcome. The outcome is therefore observed for about 37 per cent of surviving cohort members (56 of 152 or 153), or 43 per cent if the printed 66 is used. The observed differ from the unobserved: 'Significant differences were observed in terms of age at baseline, the time in current high-security admission prior to baseline, and the total length of time as a psychiatric inpatient. The group that provided data for the study demonstrated higher median scores', and those outside Scotland 'were excluded from the analysis'. Because the observed proportion is zero, any paid work among the unobserved survivors, who include people who left Scotland or left mental health and general practitioner services, could only raise it.

rationale: The result is one narrative sentence: 'at the 20 year follow-up, no participants were in paid employment, with 11.1% in some form of supported work style placement'. Remuneration is explicit and paid employment is separated from supported placements, which favours validity of the construct. But the paper does not state how employment status was identified (participant interview, case note review or keyworker report), gives no reference period and no definition or instrument for the item, and defers its tools to supplementary appendices and an earlier protocol paper that were not available to this appraisal. The Discussion wording, 'no reviewed individuals in paid employment', suggests case note review but does not establish it. The baseline primary diagnoses in Table 1 describe the cohort, and eligibility was detention in the State Hospital; neither establishes the validity of the employment condition.

rationale: Data sources differed between participants: of the 66 consenting, 48 had interview plus case note review and 18 case note review only, and the author reply indicates that the reported base also drew on case notes of 16 deceased cohort members. rationale: A simple proportion is the appropriate analysis for a prevalence figure, but the paper gives it as narrative only: a zero with no stated denominator and no interval, beside a percentage (11.1 per cent in supported placements) whose base is not given. The author reply supplies the base as 72 = 56 living consented + 16 deceased with accessible notes. A base mixing living and deceased people is not appropriate for point prevalence of current paid work, although with a zero numerator the proportion is unaffected (0 of 72 implies 0 of 56) and only its precision changes. 11.1 per cent equals 8 of 72 and is not an integer count of 56 or of 66, which is consistent with the 72 base without proving it (6 of 54 and 7 of 63 give the same percentage). The paper's own count of 66 consenting (48 interviewed, 18 case note review only) is not reconciled with the author's 56. No adjustment is made for the selective participation shown in the baseline comparison.

rationale: The printed 'Overall participation rate' of 75.9 per cent (66/87) is conditional on gatekeeper approval. Against surviving cohort members it is about 43 per cent (66 of 153), and about 37 per cent for this outcome (56 of 152 or 153, author reply). Non-participation comprises 21 who were invited and did not consent, 37 not approached because a clinician judged them to lack capacity or to be too unwell, 21 outside Scotland and 8 with no gatekeeper or lost. Management is limited to a baseline comparison of contributors with those too unwell, refusing or lost, which found significant differences in age and in length of high-security and total inpatient stay; cohort members outside Scotland were left out of that comparison. No weighting, bounds or sensitivity analysis is applied to the employment figure. With an observed proportion of zero, non-response can only have lowered the estimate.
